title: How do you come across as clear and calm in a case interview?
description: The half of the interview most candidates never train: voice, composure and business fluency.
hook: You come across as clear and calm by giving the answer first, speaking in short sentences at a steady pace, and pausing instead of filling silence with "um". All the way through your case, the interviewer is asking a quiet question: would I put this person in front of a client? That is not about being polished or extroverted, and every habit that answers it well can be practised in 10 to 20 minutes a day.

In this guide

  • Why this matters as much as the maths

  • Common mistakes
  • A daily routine
  • Practise it

Why this matters as much as the maths

Two candidates with the same structure and the same numbers can get different results. One speaks in calm, well-paced sentences and pauses before answering. The other rushes, fills silences with "um" and "like", and loses the thread when a number surprises them. The interviewer is picturing each of them presenting to a chief executive next month.

The good news is that none of this is personality. Accent, speaking speed and how outgoing you are vary from person to person, and none of them measures your thinking. What matters is that someone who has not seen your notes can follow you easily.

Clarity starts with structure

Most unclear answers are not badly spoken. They are badly ordered. Compare these two:

The sales figure is lower and I think maybe it could be competition or prices, and I'd also want to look at advertising.
Sales fell because order volume declined; average price held steady. I'll look at customer retention first, then acquisition.

The second is easier to follow because it separates what the evidence shows from what you will test next. That is the pyramid principle at sentence level: the point first, then the reasons, then the next step.

Use three building blocks for almost everything you say in a case:

  1. Headline. One sentence that answers the question you were asked.
  2. Support. Two or three reasons or numbers, in a stated order ("two reasons: first... second...").
  3. Next step. What you want to look at now, and why.

Voice: pace, pauses and no fillers

Slow down slightly

Nerves speed most people up. Aim for a pace a little slower than feels natural, especially when you say numbers. Read a business article aloud for five minutes, pausing at every full stop, and you will start to feel the right speed.

Replace fillers with pauses

A short silent pause sounds confident. "Um", "like" and "basically" sound nervous, and they make your sentences longer without adding meaning. Record a two-minute answer, count your fillers, then record it again with a silent pause wherever a filler was.

Say numbers with their units

"Seven point six" means nothing. "7.6% of revenue" or "$2.4M a year" is a complete thought. Finish every calculation by saying what it means for the client.

Holding the thread under pressure

Mid-case you are juggling the client's goal, your structure, three numbers and the next step, while talking. Two habits help.

  • Write the goal at the top of your page, in a box, with the key numbers beside it. After each calculation, glance at it and link the result back.
  • Recover in one sentence. If you lose your place, restate the objective and the last finding, then propose the next step: "We're trying to restore profit to $5M. We now know costs, not revenue, drove the fall. So I'd like to break costs down next."

A short thoughtful pause is always better than filling the space with an ever longer sentence.

Staying calm in your body

A calm voice starts with calm breathing. Before every mock and the real interview, many people find two minutes of slow breathing helps: box breathing (in for four counts, hold for four, out for four, hold for four), or simply breathing out for longer than you breathe in. Sit upright, keep your hands still on the table, and look at the interviewer when you give a headline. If nerves are a big issue for you, the guide to staying calm when nerves hit goes further.

A worked example: the same insight, two ways

Suppose a restaurant chain has $40M of revenue and profit has fallen by $3M. You have just found that delivery commissions rose from 1.5% to 7.6% of revenue.

First, the maths. At 1.5%, commissions cost 0.015 × $40M = $0.6M. At 7.6%, they cost 0.076 × $40M = $3.04M. The increase is $3.04M − $0.6M = $2.44M, which is about 81% of the $3M profit drop.

Rushed:

So, um, I think like the main thing is basically costs, because, um, the delivery thing, like, they pay a lot of commission and stuff, so that's probably most of it.

Composed:

The main driver is delivery commissions. [pause] They rose from 1.5% to 7.6% of revenue, which is about $2.4M of extra cost a year. That explains roughly 80% of the $3M profit drop. Next, I'd like to check whether delivery orders bring in enough extra revenue to justify that cost.

Same idea. The second has a headline, a number with its unit, a "so what" and a next step, and it sounds like someone you could put in front of a client.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking aloud in a stream. Saying every half-formed thought makes you hard to follow. Ask for 20 seconds, then give the organised version.
  • Burying the answer. If your conclusion is in your last sentence, the interviewer has stopped listening. Move it to the first.
  • Reading your notes aloud. Look up, say the headline, then glance down for numbers.
  • Over-apologising. If you make an error, correct it once ("Sorry, that's $2.4M, not $24M") and move on.
  • Performing a "consultant voice". Borrowed jargon and a put-on tone sound less confident, not more. Speak like yourself, in short sentences.

A daily routine

These habits compound with short, regular practice. Ten to twenty minutes most days does more than two hours on a Sunday.

ExerciseTimeWhat it trains
Read a business article aloud, slightly slowly5 minPace
Record a 2-minute answer, re-record without fillers5 minPauses
Explain one chart in 45 seconds, answer first3 minStructure under time pressure
Recap a 2-minute podcast clip in 60 seconds5 minHolding the thread
Two minutes of slow breathing2 minCalm

When you listen back to a recording, check four things: an answer-first opening, accurate numbers with units, a pause between ideas and a concrete next step.

Practise it

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. What is the best replacement for a filler word like "um": speaking faster, a short silent pause, or saying "basically"?

Show the answer

A short silent pause. It reads as confidence and gives you thinking time.

2. Rewrite this so it is answer first: "We looked at prices, which are flat, and volumes, which are down 12%, and competitors are also flat, so I think the issue is volume."

Show the answer

"The issue is volume: it is down 12%, while our prices and competitors' are flat. I'd like to find out which customers we are losing."

3. Record yourself answering "Why consulting?" for 60 seconds. Count your fillers, then record it again with a pause wherever a filler was.

Show the answer

Aim for fewer than three fillers a minute. A clean shape is a one-sentence answer, two reasons each backed by a moment from your own experience, and a close that links to the firm you are speaking to.

Where to practise next

Use the exercises on the interview skills page and the guide to speaking more clearly. To rehearse what to say at each moment of a case, try the phrase trainer on perfect casing, and practise 45-second chart explanations with the chart drill.
